title: Successive Electronic Topological Transitions in the Antiferromagnet UPd$_2$Al$_3$
authors: Adrien Gourgout, Gaël Bastien, Dai Aoki, Gabriel Seyfarth, Ilya Sheikin, Andrey Varlamov, Gertrud Zwicknagl, Jacques Flouquet, Georg Knebel, Alexandre Pourret
abstract: We report successive anomalies at low temperature in the magnetic field dependence of the thermoelectric signal in the heavy fermion compound UPd$_{2}$Al$_{3}$ inside the antiferromagnetic state up to the metamagnetic transition at $H_\text{M} =18$~T. Based on renormalisation perturbation theory and the partitioning of the $f$ orbitals into localized and delocalized parts, our analysis attributes these anomalies to complex topological changes of the Fermi surface driven by Zeeman effect. The observation of a sudden change of sign both in the thermoelectric power and in the Hall coefficient at $H_\text{M}$ in addition to the appearance of large quantum oscillations in the thermoelectric power above $H_\text{M}$ indicate a strong Fermi surface reconstruction at the metamagnetic transition due to the unfolding of the electronic bands.
summary: This paper reports on evidence of successive electronic topological transitions in UPd2Al3 as it moves from an antiferromagnetic to a paramagnetic state under high magnetic fields. By analyzing sharp anomalies in thermoelectric power and Hall measurements, the authors argue for a strong Fermi surface reconstruction at the metamagnetic transition. The combination of transport diagnostics and theoretical modeling highlights how field-induced changes govern the electronic properties of heavy fermion systems.
main_problem: The study investigates successive electronic topological transitions (ETTs) occurring in the antiferromagnetic state of the heavy fermion compound UPd2Al3 when subjected to a high external magnetic field.
main_result: The anomalies observed, particularly the sign change in thermoelectric power and Hall coefficient at the metamagnetic transition ($H_M$), strongly indicate a drastic Fermi surface reconstruction driven by band unfolding. This suggests that topological changes are key features of correlated electron behavior in this material.
method: The research combines experimental measurements (thermoelectric power, Hall effect, dHvA oscillations) with theoretical analysis using renormalization perturbation theory to model the electronic structure changes.
model_or_system: The physical system is the heavy fermion compound UPd2Al3, which exhibits antiferromagnetism and superconductivity. The focus is on understanding how its Fermi surface topology evolves across magnetic phase transitions (AF $\leftrightarrow$ PPM) under external fields.
key_observables: Thermoelectric power (Seebeck coefficient $S$), Hall coefficient ($ho_{xy}$), quantum oscillation frequencies, and effective masses ($m^*$).
important_parameters: Magnetic field strength up to 35 T; critical temperatures like Néel temperature ($T_N = 14.5 	ext{ K}$) and superconducting transition temperature ($T_{SC} = 2 	ext{ K}$).
main_assumptions: The anomalies are attributed to complex topological changes in the Fermi surface driven by the Zeeman effect, suggesting a connection between magnetic field tuning and Lifshitz transitions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate temperature dependence of $S(T)$ showing kinks at $T_N$ and steps at $T_{SC}$; magnetoresistance/Hall measurements show anomalies at $H_M$; and FFT analysis reveals quantum oscillation frequencies above $H_M$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents transport measurements across the AF to PPM transition, using multiple diagnostics (TEP, Hall effect) to pinpoint the metamagnetic field ($H_M$). Theoretical modeling is then used to interpret these sharp changes as evidence of Fermi surface reconstruction.
why_interesting: This work exemplifies how high-field magnetotransport measurements are crucial for mapping out complex electronic phase diagrams in strongly correlated materials, providing signatures (like sign changes and quantum oscillations) that point toward fundamental topological changes in the band structure.
